title: The Bicycle Duty
logline: You are Maren Vos's lawyer. At dawn, a truck of her bicycles from Germania was stopped at the border of Nederlanda: a brand-new national statute has brought back a customs duty on imports. Her small import firm, Kade Freight, will go under if she pays. Tonight, at the District Court of Nederlanda, you have one night to show that a single phrase of the TFEU gives her a right the court must protect, even against a newer statute.
learning_goal: By the end, the player can: 1. Identify the precise Treaty provision, not just the Article, and cite it as "Article X(y)(z) TFEU" [L1 p.7], [L1 p.28], [T1 p.10]. 2. Apply the three Van Gend & Loos requirements one at a time: clear, unconditional, and adapted to produce direct effects in the legal relationship between Member States and their subjects [L1 p.25], [L1 p.29], [WA1 p.1]. 3. Only after direct effect is established, apply supremacy: a later national law cannot prevail (Costa v ENEL) [L1 p.26], [L1 p.27]. The national court must disapply it of its own motion, without waiting for the legislator or the constitutional court (Simmenthal II) [L4 p.21], [L4 p.24], [L4 p.30]. 4. Avoid the "typical error" of jumping straight to supremacy without testing direct effect [L1 p.30], [T1 p.9].

The lit entrance is the customs booth's glass door, its window lit from inside.

The player's case-file PDA carries forward from the yard: client name, the truck, the duty notice, and the Treaty provision once it is found.

scenes.title: The Provision
action: Pale oak panelling, a raised bench. JUDGE DE WIT presides. MR. HAAN stands for the customs authority. The lawyer stands beside MAREN, the TFEU book open, printed judgment pages striped with sodium-amber highlighter beside it.

dialogue.speaker: JUDGE DE WIT
dialogue.line: Counsel for the claimant. Tell me your client has a right. Not a hope. A right.

dialogue.speaker: LAWYER
dialogue.line: Then we don't start with "EU law beats national law." We start with one phrase. (finger on page) Article 30, first phrase, TFEU. "Customs duties on imports and exports ... shall be prohibited between Member States."

dialogue.speaker: HAAN
dialogue.line: Your Honour, that Article speaks to Member States. My client's officers were only enforcing a statute passed by Parliament.

dialogue.speaker: LAWYER
dialogue.line: Before sixty-three, most lawyers thought so too. The Court said the Treaty is more than mutual obligations between States. It's a new legal order, and its subjects include their nationals.

dialogue.speaker: HAAN
dialogue.line: And that covers a company?

dialogue.speaker: LAWYER
dialogue.line: In the Court's language, "individuals" means everyone who isn't a public authority. Businesses included.

dialogue.speaker: HAAN
dialogue.line: So every article of the Treaty is a right for your client?

dialogue.speaker: JUDGE DE WIT
dialogue.line: No — and Counsel knows it. It has to pass three tests. Run them for me now.

quiz.question: Nederlanda's 2026 statute imposes a customs duty on bicycles imported from Germania. Does Kade Freight have a right under EU law that the national court must protect? Choose the answer that would score on the exam.

options.text: Yes. Article 30, first phrase, TFEU prohibits customs duties on imports between Member States. Applying Van Gend & Loos: the provision is clear, it is unconditional, and it is by nature adapted to operate between the State and its subjects. It therefore has direct effect, and Kade Freight has a right.
Yes. EU law is supreme over national law (Costa v ENEL), so the national duty simply falls away. No need to test direct effect.
options.story: the lawyer pitches "Costa v ENEL, solved!" Mr. Haan doesn't even need to rise. "Counsel hasn't shown this provision gives her client anything at all," he says, and the duty notice on the case-file HUD stamps "UPHELD" in verdict red.
options.teaching: This is the typical exam error the lecture warns about. Supremacy cannot be used to get around a provision's lack of clarity or unconditionality. If a provision does not meet all the requirements for direct effect, the court cannot disapply national law. Jumping to supremacy scores zero [L1 p.30], [T1 p.9], [WG1 p.4].

options.text: No. The Treaty only creates obligations between the States. A private company can't claim rights from it; only the Commission or another State can act.
options.story: Judge De Wit looks past the lawyer to Maren. "Then this court has nothing for you tonight." The case-file HUD flags the € 4 800 figure as due.
options.teaching: This was the pre-1963 view, and Van Gend & Loos rejected it. The Treaty is "more than an agreement which merely creates mutual obligations between the contracting states". Its subjects include nationals, and the State being the one bound "does not imply that their nationals cannot benefit" [L1 p.22], [L1 p.23], [L1 p.24], [WA1 p.1].

options.text: Yes. The Treaty is binding, so every Treaty Article gives rights to individuals. Article 28 TFEU covers customs, so Kade Freight can rely on it.
options.story: Judge De Wit flips through the TFEU: "Which phrase, counsel? Article 28 has more than one." The tab slips from the book.
options.teaching: Only some Treaty provisions have direct effect, and only if they pass all three tests. Many clear, unconditional provisions still don't concern the State–individual relationship [L1 p.23], [L1 p.25], [WA1 p.1]. An Article can contain several provisions, and you must name the exact phrase, with paragraph and "TFEU", or lose points [L1 p.7], [L1 p.28], [T1 p.10].

irac.issue: Can Kade Freight, a private company and so an "individual" in the Court's terms [L1 p.22], rely on a Treaty provision against a customs duty imposed by Nederlanda? The exam frames this as "Does X have a right under EU law?", which is a question of direct effect [L1 p.29], [T1 p.9-10].
irac.rule: Article 30, first phrase, TFEU: customs duties on imports and exports between Member States are prohibited [L1 p.20]. Following Van Gend & Loos, a Treaty provision creates rights for individuals that national courts must protect only if it is (1) clear, (2) unconditional, meaning it needs no further implementation by EU or national rules, and (3) by its nature "adapted to produce direct effects in the legal relationship between Member States and their subjects" [L1 p.25], [WA1 p.1], [WG1 p.5-6]. Cite the provision precisely: Article, paragraph or phrase, and "TFEU" [L1 p.28], [T1 p.10].
irac.application: Base each requirement on how the provision is worded [L1 p.29]. Clear: it names exactly what is banned (customs duties on imports and exports) and between whom (Member States). Unconditional: nothing in the phrase makes the ban depend on a further EU or national measure. This mirrors the Court's reading of its predecessor, Article 12 EEC, as a "clear and unconditional prohibition" not qualified by any reservation requiring national legislation [L1 p.24]. Adapted: it is a negative obligation on the State that operates at the national level, at the border between the State and the importer. That the Member States are the addressees "does not imply that their nationals cannot benefit" [L1 p.24].
irac.conclusion: Article 30, first phrase, TFEU has direct effect. Kade Freight has a right under EU law that the national court must protect [L1 p.21], [L1 p.25].

scenes.title: Newer Than the Treaty
action: Same courtroom, moments later, the gold "SUSTAINED" card still fading from the case-file HUD. Mr. Haan rises again for the customs authority.

dialogue.speaker: HAAN
dialogue.line: Your Honour, the Import Duty Act dates from 2026. The Treaty is decades older. The later law prevails.

dialogue.speaker: LAWYER
dialogue.line: The Court of Justice rejected that argument in 1964. Treaty law can't be overridden by domestic provisions, "however framed".

dialogue.speaker: HAAN
dialogue.line: Then let Parliament repeal the Act, or let the Constitutional Court strike it down. This court cannot simply ignore a statute.

dialogue.speaker: JUDGE DE WIT
dialogue.line: (to the lawyer) Counsel. Suppose I accept that Article 30, first phrase, has direct effect. What exactly am I obliged to do with this statute, and when?

quiz.question: Article 30, first phrase, TFEU has been shown to have direct effect. The conflicting national statute is later than the Treaty, and the State says only Parliament or the Constitutional Court can remove it. What must the District Court do?

options.text: Of its own motion, refuse to apply the conflicting duty right away, without waiting for Parliament or the Constitutional Court. It does not matter that the statute is later, because the EU provision meets all the requirements for direct effect.
Apply the 2026 statute. Under lex posterior, a later national law prevails over an older Treaty.
options.story: the judge nods to Haan, and the gavel falls. Cut to the customs yard: a clamp locks onto the truck's wheel.
options.teaching: Before 1964 the view was that the rank of Community law depended on national rules, so a later national law could prevail. Costa v ENEL ended that: a national rule can never prevail over EU law, "however framed" [L1 p.26], [L1 p.27], [WA1 p.1]. Simmenthal II confirms that national law must be set aside "whether prior or subsequent" [L4 p.22].

options.text: Stay the case until Parliament repeals the Act or the Constitutional Court declares it unconstitutional. Only those bodies can remove a statute.
options.story: a calendar on the courtroom wall flips through months. The bicycle boxes gather dust in the warehouse, and Maren locks the office for the last time.
options.teaching: This was the Italian Constitutional Court's position before Simmenthal II: only repeal by the legislator or a declaration of unconstitutionality [L4 p.18]. The ECJ rejected it. The court must act of its own motion, without requesting or awaiting setting aside "by legislative or other constitutional means" [L4 p.21], [L4 p.24], [WA4 p.1].

options.text: Refuse to apply the statute, because supremacy is absolute. Whether Article 30 has direct effect is irrelevant to this question.
options.story: the judge's pen stops. "Counsel, if supremacy alone were enough, I could disapply any statute I disliked." The gold card stays grey: no points.
options.teaching: Supremacy looks absolute but is limited by direct effect. Disapplying national law without checking the requirements would be arbitrary and against the rule of law [T1 p.9]. Neither Costa v ENEL nor Simmenthal II can be used to get around a lack of clarity or unconditionality. First establish direct effect, then apply Simmenthal II [L1 p.30], [L4 p.21], [L4 p.23], [WG1 p.4].

irac.issue: Must a national court wait for the legislator or the constitutional court before it refuses to apply a later national statute that conflicts with a directly effective Treaty provision? [L4 p.19]
irac.rule: Costa v ENEL: the Treaty created its own legal system, which became an integral part of the national legal systems. Law stemming from the Treaty "could not ... be overridden by domestic legal provisions, however framed", so a later national rule cannot prevail [L1 p.26], [L1 p.27], [WA1 p.1]. Simmenthal II (Case 106/77): directly applicable EU provisions "render automatically inapplicable any conflicting provision of current national law" (para 17). Every national court must "set aside any provision of national law which may conflict with it, whether prior or subsequent" (para 21). It must refuse "of its own motion" to apply it, and need not "request or await the prior setting aside of such provision by legislative or other constitutional means" (para 24) [L4 p.20], [L4 p.21], [L4 p.22], [L4 p.24], [WA4 p.1]. These duties exist only if the EU provision meets all the requirements for direct effect [L4 p.21], [L4 p.23], [L1 p.30]. In the exam, Simmenthal II must be applied where a party argues that the court has to wait for the constitutional court or the legislator [L4 p.30].
irac.application: Examination I established that Article 30, first phrase, TFEU is clear, unconditional and adapted, so it has direct effect. The duty imposed by the 2026 Act conflicts with it. That the Act is later than the Treaty makes no difference ("prior or subsequent"). Mr. Haan's argument that Parliament or the Constitutional Court must act first is the argument Simmenthal II rejects [L4 p.18], [L4 p.21].
irac.conclusion: The District Court must, of its own motion and immediately, refuse to apply the duty to Kade Freight. The conflicting rule is automatically inapplicable, and the court does not wait for any national measure [L5 p.21], [L4 p.24].

dialogue.speaker: JUDGE DE WIT
dialogue.line: On the claim before me tonight: the Import Duty Act 2026, as applied to Kade Freight's shipment, is set aside, with immediate effect, of this court's own motion. The customs authority will release the load. (beat) Counsel — well argued.

"A clear, unconditional Treaty phrase creates a right the moment it applies — check the three tests before you ever mention supremacy. And once direct effect is established, a national court must set aside a conflicting statute right away, however new it is, and however framed."
Next case: Week 2 — legislative procedures and horizontal effect.

case_file: Claimant: Maren Vos, MD, Kade Freight (import firm).
Claim: a right against the Import Duty Act 2026 (Nederlanda), a customs duty on goods from Germania.
Exhibit flagged: duty notice, € 4 800, statute in force since Monday.

irac.issue: Does Kade Freight have a right under EU law against the Import Duty Act 2026?
irac.rule: Van Gend & Loos: a Treaty provision has direct effect if it is clear, unconditional, and adapted to produce direct effects between Member States and their subjects [L1 p.25], [WA1 p.1].
irac.application: Article 30, first phrase, TFEU is clear, unconditional and adapted; the State being the named addressee does not stop Kade Freight, an "individual", from benefiting [L1 p.22], [L1 p.24].
irac.conclusion: Article 30, first phrase, TFEU has direct effect. Kade Freight has a right under EU law [L1 p.21], [L1 p.25].

irac.issue: What must the District Court do about the conflicting 2026 statute, and when?
irac.rule: Costa v ENEL + Simmenthal II: a later national rule cannot prevail; the court must set it aside of its own motion, without waiting for the legislator or the constitutional court [L1 p.26], [L1 p.27], [L4 p.21], [L4 p.24].
irac.application: The duty conflicts with a directly effective Treaty provision; that the statute is newer makes no difference [L4 p.18], [L4 p.21].
irac.conclusion: The District Court must refuse to apply the duty immediately, of its own motion [L5 p.21], [L4 p.24].

verdict.takeaway: "A clear, unconditional Treaty phrase creates a right the moment it applies — check the three tests before you ever mention supremacy. And once direct effect is established, a national court must set aside a conflicting statute right away, however new it is, and however framed."

coordinator_notes: N1: Simmenthal is not a Week 1 case in IIEL. The IIEL Week 1 lecture teaches supremacy through Costa v ENEL only and says how to apply it comes in Week 6 [L1 p.30], [T1 p.10]. The IIEL lecture that teaches Simmenthal II is Week 4 [L4 p.17-30], and Week 5 restates it [L5 p.15], [L5 p.21]. The only "W1" file that mentions Simmenthal is W1 Lecture 1B slides.txt, which belongs to a different course ("Law of the European Union", Villanueva, 2026-27), even though the database tags it IIEL. Examination II uses the IIEL Week 4 slides as its authority.

N2: Course mix-up in the database. W1 Lecture 1A slides.txt, W1 Lecture 1B slides.txt and W1 Assignment.txt are tagged IIEL/rank 1 but come from "Law of the European Union 2026-27". The word "IRAC" appears only there [V1A p.1]. The IIEL sources teach the same method without the label [L1 p.29], and the resit grading splits marks into knowledge and application [SA p.4-5].

N3: Inconsistency in the Week 1 model answers. EU_Worksheet_W1_ANSWERS.docx p.1 says both "Article 108(2), third sentence" and "the third sentence of Article 108(3) TFEU" for the one directly effective provision. The quoted text is paragraph 3. This game avoids the Article 108 example because of this.
N4: Minor slide typo. [L1 p.8] headed "ARTICLE 13 TFEU", but [L1 p.7], [T1 p.5] and [WG1 p.5] say Article 13 TEU. Not used in the game.

N5: European Law WG Week 1.pdf is a written answer set that says it draws partly on "supporting course notes". It was used only where it matches L1 or WA1. - Lower-ranked sources: none relied on. Rank 1 covered every claim.
